Expiate

/EK-spee-ayt/ - the stress falls on EK · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Expiate means to make amends for a wrong; to atone.

Decades after the false expulsion, the old headmaster tried to expiate his injustice by endowing a scholarship in the wronged student's name.

Worked Example

The shepherd whose carelessness let fire into the common pasture never disputed the fine; he spent the next three springs reseeding the hillsides at his own cost, determined to expiate the loss in full.

Expiate is stronger than 'apologize' and more concrete than 'repent': it means paying the moral debt down with real acts. And note its object — you expiate a wrong, a sin, or guilt itself, not the person you injured.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

redeem: To redeem is to buy back your good name, sometimes with a single shining act that restores you to favor. Expiate stays fixed on the wrong itself: you pay the moral debt down, act by act, until the account is settled. Redeem rescues the person; expiate settles the offense.

atone: To atone is the general word for making amends — you atone for a wrong, and a change of heart alone can count. Expiate leans harder on the outward payment: the labor, cost, or gift that settles the account. You expiate a wrong; the person you injured is never its object.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deny: to refuse to admit the wrong at all

worsen: to add to the harm instead of paying it down

Where it sits · how fully the wrong is paid for — apologize → repent → expiate

apologize vs. expiate: An apology costs one sentence and a moment's humility; apologize stops far short of expiate, which pays for the wrong with real acts over time.

repent vs. expiate: To repent is to feel the wrong sincerely and turn from it; repent stops short of expiate, which goes on to settle the debt in deeds.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: out, completely

Root — pi

Root — pi: dutiful; to appease

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do

Put it together

Put it together: Ex- (completely) + pi (from Latin pius, 'dutiful') + -ate (to make) = to make fully dutiful again. Roman piety was a debt owed to gods and family; expiare meant paying that debt after a wrong. To expiate is still exactly that — squaring the moral account.

Use the root in a new word: piety

Use the root in a new word: piety: Her piety showed less in loud prayers than in the quiet duties she never once skipped.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Expiate keeps company with sin, guilt, and old wrongs — sermons and novels more than newsrooms. You met atone earlier in this course; the two overlap closely, but expiate leans harder on the outward payment, the labor or gift that settles the account.
